current_text.html: Subject to the provisions below, after the higher court has decided that the notice filed with its clerk was timely and that the complaint is otherwise in order for it to be heard by the higher court, it shall hear the complaint, or in accordance with the provision of BCO 15-2 and 15-3, appoint a commission to do so. Ordinarily the court or its commission shall schedule a hearing in a manner that reasonably accommodates the schedules of the respective parties and affords each party a prior opportunity to file a written brief upon such terms and in accord with a briefing schedule established by the court or its commission in the reasonable exercise of its discretion.

relationships.title: Biese et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

2. Did Grace Presbytery err under BCO 43-8 in appointing the Commission to hear December 21 Blue Hen complaint due to that complaint being moot and thereby administratively out of order under BCO 43-3?

metadata.synopsis: Case 2023-08 was adjudicated with Case 2023-06 in the Baird complaints against Grace Presbytery. The SJC sustained the complaints in the main, rejected one specification, and did not reach another; concurring opinions were recorded.

relationships.title: Mueller v. South Florida Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: On complaint by RE William F. Mueller, the SJC reviewed whether the Redlands Community Church Session erred on January 14, 2019 by allegedly reaffirming its practice of fencing the Lord's Table contrary to BCO 58-4. The SJC denied the complaint: the only relevant motion failed for lack of a second, so the Session took no action and did not reaffirm anything. It noted the case could have been ruled out of order earlier and that Mueller could pursue relief under BCO 40-5; a concurrence stressed BCO 58-4 remains binding and criticized Presbytery's handling.

metadata.synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

metadata.synopsis: After a Session excommunicated a member without trial for contumacy, the SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the contumacy judgment, excommunication, and later Session and Presbytery actions. No mutually agreed BCO 38-1 confession existed, and declining a confession meeting was not immediately censurable objective contumacy under BCO 32-6; subjective contumacy required confession or trial. He reverted to membership under pending indictment. The SJC did not find the indictment unconstitutional, decide trial guilt, or consider the unpleaded trespass warning.

metadata.synopsis: The complaint challenged Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery’s November 17, 2012 vote adopting its Complaint Commission’s recommendation to institute process and try TE David Swavely. The SJC did not sustain it. Although the record showed possible procedural irregularities—including unauthorized circulation of an earlier complaint—the SJC found no reversible error: presbyteries receive deference on factual records and broad latitude to judge the sufficiency of investigations. The recommendation to proceed to trial stands, subject to later parliamentary action. The SJC did not decide Swavely’s guilt.

metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained the Session's complaint against Presbytery. Presbytery had ruled a member's original complaint administratively out of order as untimely but then remanded the matter to the Session; the SJC held that once out of order, no complaint remained to remand. It also held Presbytery could not direct or instruct the Session to initiate formal process without BCO 40-5's required citation step, so those directions were null and void. The member remained under the Session's jurisdiction; the civil trespass order was not ecclesiastical discipline and did not alter membership.

relationships.title: Dunn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: The SJC held TE Dwight Dunn's complaint administratively out of order under OMSJC 9.1 and directed Presbytery to remedy the deficiencies by its next Stated Meeting before further action under OMSJC 9.2. The original complaint had been transmitted to the Faith Church Commission by the Stated Clerk, not committed by Presbytery motion as BCO 15-3 requires, and after the Commission denied it, the Commission did not seek Presbytery approval of its judgment. Because Presbytery had not acted, the SJC complaint was premature; no merits were reached.

relationships.title: Sherfey v. James River Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Sherfey challenged James River Presbytery’s denial of his complaint and alleged errors in its commission’s proceedings. The SJC ruled the complaint judicially out of order with incurable defects: several grounds had not first been adjudicated by Presbytery as BCO 43-2 required, and the General Assembly filing missed BCO 43-3’s thirty-day deadline. Incorrect advice from Presbytery’s clerk did not excuse compliance. The adopted decision neither reached the merits nor ordered a remand; only a concurrence proposed returning the matter to Presbytery.

metadata.synopsis: A complaint challenging Northwest Georgia Presbytery’s denial of Laura Wood’s complaint against a session was declared judicially out of order and dismissed because Presbytery later rescinded the challenged action; the SJC said the defects could not be cured and no grounds remained. It reached no merits. The dissent argued rescission did not automatically defeat a complaint and that her complaint also alleged Presbytery’s failure to act.

relationships.title: Armes v. Southwest Florida Presbytery

occurrences.excerpt: For the reasons set forth herein, the Complaint is sustained, and the matter is remanded to the Southwest Florida Presbytery with direction to proceed in accordance with BCO 43-8 to hear the Complaint, or appoint a Commission to do the same.

metadata.synopsis: Southwest Florida Presbytery denied Armes's second complaint as a mere restatement of Case 2009-12; the SJC sustained the complaint and remanded, finding the second complaint involved distinct post-censure acts (the trespass notice) that could not be dismissed as identical in substance. A dissenting opinion argued Armes, as an excommunicated person, lacked standing to bring any complaint beyond the limited access afforded under BCO 38-1.

relationships.title: Smith v. Southwest Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: Smith appealed discipline for divisiveness, gossip and slander, broken membership vows, and contumacy arising largely from complaints and letters during church conflict. The SJC sustained her appeal, reversed guilt on all four charges, and annulled suspension from the sacraments. The documentary record proved none of the allegations; filing complaints was not itself divisiveness, and the trial improperly lacked a witness, shifted proof to Smith, showed prejudice, and unfairly rejected her written defense. The SJC declined remand because the evidence was insufficient.

topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
suspension from office without due process
metadata.synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.
